newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn, Paris divided on budget pact as summit looms.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, Paris divided on budget pact as summit looms.

text.p: Negotiations on a budget pact to ensure fiscal discipline within Europe's single currency on Monday looked set for a cliffhanger ending as Germany and France clearly failed to agree a joint position.

German chancellor Helmut Kohl told a news conference at the end of a one-day summit in the German city of Nuremberg that the two countries planned to reveal a joint position on a European budget pact in the next few days.
But he gave no evidence they the two sides had moved even slightly closer to resolving their differences on the issue.
"French and German finance ministers are in the middle of important working groups and want to prepare a joint initiative and consult other European Union ministers before Thursday," Kohl said.
"It will concern the long-term stability of the future currency, the future EMS2 relationships and a series of legal issues," he added.

Germany has found itself at odds with France and other European Union nations on the terms of a so-called stability pact, intended to ensure countries entering European Economic and Monetary Union in 1999 keep budget spending under control.

At the centre of the dispute is Bonn's insistence on strict numerical definitions of the 'temporary and extraordinary' circumstances which will allow a nation to overshoot a maximum deficit level of three percent of gross domestic product.
Germany has argued that such a definition is needed to avoid loopholes of political compromise in the pact.
Protests from France and others that the definitions Germany is seeking are too rigid has only redoubled Bonn's determination to make the pact as watertight as possible.
One delegation source said that there had been almost no progress on the issue in Nuremberg.

The persistent division of the Franco-German axis means that time is now running out if the European Union wants to meet its stated goal of agreeing at least the broad terms of the pact at a summit of EU leaders in Dublin this week.
European economic and finance ministers failed to agree on a deal for the pact -- which will impose sanctions and then fines on offenders -- at a meeting in Brussels last Monday.
They will meet again on Thursday in a last-ditch attempt to agree the framework of a pact before the Dublin summit.

Stressing nonetheless that there was complete agreement between France and Germany on central parts of the single currency project, Kohl said that both parties wanted the single European currency to be strong.
"Neither France nor Germany want a weak currency," he said.
He added that it made no sense to speculate on what nations would be initial members in the currency union.
